description: Comprehensive question bank derived from Earth Science and Geological Science study material for FDA & SDA competitive examination preparation. Covers Earth structure, geological processes, meteorology, climate, and hydrology.

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What is the approximate age of the Earth?

options.A: 4.54 million years

questions.explanation: Earth formed about 4.54 billion years ago, based mainly on radiometric dating of meteorites and the oldest terrestrial and lunar materials.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What is the nebular hypothesis?

options.A: A model stating that the Solar System formed from a rotating cloud of gas and dust that collapsed under gravity
options.B: A theory that Earth was created by a giant impact
options.C: A hypothesis that planets were captured from another star
options.D: A model explaining the origin of life on Earth

questions.explanation: The nebular hypothesis states that the Solar System formed from a rotating cloud of gas and dust that collapsed under gravity, producing the Sun and a disk from which planets formed.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: Why is Earth called a terrestrial planet?

options.A: Because it has a gaseous surface
options.B: Because it is a relatively dense, rocky planet with a solid surface
options.C: Because it has rings around it
options.D: Because it is the largest planet in the Solar System

questions.explanation: Earth is called a terrestrial planet because it is a relatively dense, rocky planet with a solid surface, unlike the giant gas and ice planets.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What are the three main compositional layers of Earth?

options.A: Lithosphere, asthenosphere, mesosphere

questions.explanation: Earth is commonly divided compositionally into crust, mantle and core.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What is the thickness of continental crust?
questions.explanation: Continental crust is commonly about 30-70 km thick, with substantial variation; it is generally thicker beneath major mountain belts.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What is the thickness of oceanic crust?
questions.explanation: Oceanic crust is generally about 5-10 km thick, thinner and denser than continental crust.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What is the mantle?

options.A: The thin outermost solid layer of Earth
options.B: The thick layer between the crust and core, extending to about 2,900 km depth
options.C: The central metallic region of Earth
options.D: The rigid outer shell broken into tectonic plates

questions.explanation: The mantle is the thick layer between the crust and core, extending to about 2,900 km depth. It consists mainly of solid silicate rocks that can deform and flow slowly over geological time.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: Is the mantle a liquid layer?

options.A: Yes, it is completely liquid
options.B: No, most of the mantle is solid but behaves plastically over long periods
options.C: Yes, it is a global ocean of liquid magma
options.D: No, it is completely rigid and cannot deform

questions.explanation: No. Most of the mantle is solid, although it behaves plastically over long periods; local partial melting occurs in some regions.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What is the core of Earth composed of?

options.A: Silicate rocks

questions.explanation: Earth's central metallic region is composed mainly of iron and nickel, divided into a liquid outer core and solid inner core.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What is the outer core?

options.A: A solid iron-rich layer from 2,900 km to 5,150 km depth
options.B: A liquid iron-rich layer extending from about 2,900 km to 5,150 km depth
options.C: The solid central part of Earth from 5,150 km to the centre
options.D: The uppermost part of the mantle

questions.explanation: The outer core is a liquid iron-rich layer extending from about 2,900 km to 5,150 km depth; its movement helps generate Earth's magnetic field.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What is the inner core?

options.A: A liquid iron-rich layer
options.B: The solid, iron-rich central part of Earth extending from about 5,150 km depth to the centre
options.C: The layer between the crust and mantle
options.D: The rigid outer shell of Earth

questions.explanation: The inner core is the solid, iron-rich central part of Earth, extending from about 5,150 km depth to the centre at roughly 6,371 km.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What is the lithosphere?

options.A: A relatively weak, deformable zone in the upper mantle
options.B: The rigid outer shell consisting of the crust and the uppermost mantle

questions.explanation: The lithosphere is the rigid outer shell consisting of the crust and the uppermost mantle; it is broken into tectonic plates.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What is the asthenosphere?

options.A: The rigid outer shell of Earth
options.B: A relatively weak, deformable zone in the upper mantle beneath the lithosphere

questions.explanation: The asthenosphere is a relatively weak, deformable zone in the upper mantle beneath the lithosphere, over which tectonic plates move.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: How do scientists study Earth's interior?

options.A: By drilling to the core
options.B: By analysing seismic waves, gravity, magnetic fields, heat flow, meteorites and laboratory experiments

questions.explanation: Scientists study Earth's interior by analysing seismic waves, gravity, magnetic fields, heat flow, meteorites and laboratory experiments on minerals at high pressure and temperature.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What are seismic waves?

options.A: Ocean waves caused by tides
options.B: Energy waves generated by earthquakes or other sources that travel through Earth or along its surface

questions.explanation: Seismic waves are energy waves generated by earthquakes or other sources that travel through Earth or along its surface.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What is the difference between P-waves and S-waves?

options.A: P-waves are shear waves; S-waves are compressional waves
options.B: P-waves are compressional waves and travel through solids, liquids and gases; S-waves are shear waves and travel only through solids
options.C: P-waves travel only through solids; S-waves travel through all media

questions.explanation: P-waves are compressional waves and travel through solids, liquids and gases; S-waves are shear waves and travel only through solids.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: How do seismic waves provide evidence for Earth's layers?

options.A: By changing colour as they pass through layers
options.B: Changes in wave speed, reflection, refraction and the absence of S-waves through the outer core reveal internal boundaries and the liquid nature of the outer core
options.C: By stopping completely at the crust
options.D: By travelling only along the surface

questions.explanation: Changes in wave speed, reflection, refraction and the absence of S-waves through the outer core reveal internal boundaries and the liquid nature of the outer core.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What are rocks?

options.A: Loose particles of soil
options.B: Naturally occurring solid aggregates of one or more minerals or mineraloids

questions.explanation: Rocks are naturally occurring solid aggregates of one or more minerals or mineraloids that form part of Earth's crust and upper mantle.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What are the three major rock groups?

options.A: Granite, basalt, marble

questions.explanation: The three major rock groups are igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What are igneous rocks?

options.A: Rocks formed by deposition and compaction of sediments
options.B: Rocks formed by the cooling and solidification of magma or lava
options.C: Rocks altered by heat and pressure

questions.explanation: Igneous rocks are formed by the cooling and solidification of magma below the surface or lava at the surface.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What are intrusive igneous rocks?

options.A: Rocks that cool rapidly at the surface
options.B: Rocks that cool slowly beneath Earth's surface, commonly developing large crystals

questions.explanation: Intrusive igneous rocks cool slowly beneath Earth's surface, commonly developing large crystals; granite is a common example.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What are extrusive igneous rocks?

options.A: Rocks that cool slowly beneath the surface
options.B: Rocks formed when lava cools at or near the surface, commonly forming fine-grained or glassy textures

questions.explanation: Extrusive igneous rocks are formed when lava cools at or near the surface, commonly cooling rapidly and forming fine-grained or glassy textures; basalt is a common example.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: Which of the following is a common intrusive igneous rock?

options.A: Basalt

questions.explanation: Granite is a common intrusive igneous rock.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: Which of the following is a common extrusive igneous rock?

options.A: Granite

questions.explanation: Basalt is a common extrusive igneous rock.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: Give examples of igneous rocks.

options.A: Marble, slate, quartzite
options.B: Granite, basalt, gabbro, rhyolite, obsidian and pumice

questions.explanation: Examples of igneous rocks include granite, basalt, gabbro, rhyolite, obsidian and pumice.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What are sedimentary rocks?

options.A: Rocks formed by cooling of magma
options.B: Rocks formed by deposition, compaction and cementation of sediments, or by chemical precipitation or accumulation of biological material
options.C: Rocks altered by heat and pressure

questions.explanation: Sedimentary rocks are formed by deposition, compaction and cementation of sediments, or by chemical precipitation or accumulation of biological material.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What are clastic sedimentary rocks?

options.A: Rocks formed by chemical precipitation
options.B: Rocks formed from fragments of pre-existing rocks

questions.explanation: Clastic sedimentary rocks are formed from fragments of pre-existing rocks, such as conglomerate, sandstone and shale.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What are chemical sedimentary rocks?

options.A: Rocks formed from fragments of pre-existing rocks
options.B: Rocks formed when dissolved minerals precipitate from water
options.D: Rocks formed by cooling of lava

questions.explanation: Chemical sedimentary rocks are formed when dissolved minerals precipitate from water; rock salt and some limestones are examples.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What are organic or biogenic sedimentary rocks?

options.A: Rocks formed from fragments of pre-existing rocks
options.B: Rocks formed when dissolved minerals precipitate from water
options.C: Rocks formed partly or largely from biological remains or activity
options.D: Rocks formed by cooling of magma

questions.explanation: Organic or biogenic sedimentary rocks are formed partly or largely from biological remains or activity, such as coal and many fossil-rich limestones.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What are metamorphic rocks?

options.A: Rocks formed by cooling of magma
options.B: Rocks produced when existing rocks are altered by heat, pressure and chemically active fluids without completely melting
options.C: Rocks formed by deposition of sediments

questions.explanation: Metamorphic rocks are produced when existing rocks are altered by heat, pressure and chemically active fluids without completely melting.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What is contact metamorphism?

options.A: Metamorphism over large areas associated with mountain building
options.B: Metamorphism caused mainly by heat from nearby magma intrusions, generally affecting rocks over a relatively limited area

questions.explanation: Contact metamorphism is caused mainly by heat from nearby magma intrusions, generally affecting rocks over a relatively limited area.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What is regional metamorphism?

options.A: Metamorphism caused mainly by heat from nearby magma intrusions
options.B: Metamorphism over large areas, commonly associated with mountain building and high pressure and temperature

questions.explanation: Regional metamorphism occurs over large areas, commonly associated with mountain building and high pressure and temperature.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: Which of the following is a metamorphic rock?

options.A: Granite

questions.explanation: Marble is a metamorphic rock that forms when limestone or dolostone is recrystallised during metamorphism.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: How is marble formed?

options.A: From cooling of magma
options.B: When limestone or dolostone is recrystallised during metamorphism

questions.explanation: Marble forms when limestone or dolostone is recrystallised during metamorphism.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: How is slate formed?

options.A: From cooling of lava
options.B: Commonly by low-grade metamorphism of shale or mudstone

questions.explanation: Slate commonly forms by low-grade metamorphism of shale or mudstone.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: Give examples of metamorphic rocks.

options.A: Granite, basalt, gabbro
options.B: Marble, slate, quartzite, gneiss, schist and phyllite

questions.explanation: Examples of metamorphic rocks include marble, slate, quartzite, gneiss, schist and phyllite.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What are minerals?

options.A: Naturally occurring, generally inorganic solids with an ordered internal structure and a characteristic chemical composition
options.C: Organic compounds found in living organisms

questions.explanation: Minerals are naturally occurring, generally inorganic solids with an ordered internal structure and a characteristic chemical composition or range of compositions.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What are the main properties used to identify minerals?

options.A: Colour, streak, lustre, hardness, cleavage, fracture, crystal form, density and special properties

questions.explanation: The main properties used to identify minerals include colour, streak, lustre, hardness, cleavage, fracture, crystal form, density and special properties such as magnetism or reaction with dilute acid.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What is Mohs scale of hardness?

options.A: A scale measuring mineral density
options.B: A relative scale ranking mineral scratch resistance from talc at 1 to diamond at 10

questions.explanation: Mohs scale of hardness is a relative scale ranking mineral scratch resistance from talc at 1 to diamond at 10; it is not a linear scale.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What is the streak of a mineral?

options.A: The colour of a mineral's powdered form
options.B: The way a mineral reflects light
options.C: The tendency of a mineral to break along planes

questions.explanation: The streak of a mineral is the colour of a mineral's powdered form, usually observed by rubbing it on an unglazed porcelain plate.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What is cleavage in minerals?

options.A: The tendency of a mineral to break along planes of weakness in its crystal structure
options.B: The colour of a mineral's powder
options.C: The way a mineral reflects light

questions.explanation: Cleavage is the tendency of a mineral to break along planes of weakness in its crystal structure.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What is a fossil?

options.A: A type of rock formed by cooling magma
options.B: Preserved remains, impressions or traces of ancient organisms, usually found in sedimentary rocks
options.C: A mineral with a characteristic chemical composition

questions.explanation: A fossil is preserved remains, impressions or traces of ancient organisms, usually found in sedimentary rocks.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What are body fossils?

options.A: Evidence of organism activity such as footprints and burrows
options.B: Preserved parts or remains of organisms, such as bones, teeth, shells, leaves or wood

questions.explanation: Body fossils are preserved parts or remains of organisms, such as bones, teeth, shells, leaves or wood.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What are trace fossils?

options.A: Preserved bones and shells
options.B: Evidence of organism activity rather than body parts, such as footprints, burrows, trails and coprolites

questions.explanation: Trace fossils are evidence of organism activity rather than body parts, such as footprints, burrows, trails and coprolites.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: Why are fossils important?

options.A: They provide evidence of past life, evolution, ancient environments, changes in biodiversity and the relative ages of rock layers
options.C: They indicate the presence of groundwater
options.D: They are used to measure earthquake magnitude

questions.explanation: Fossils provide evidence of past life, evolution, ancient environments, changes in biodiversity and the relative ages of rock layers.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What is soil?

options.A: A natural body of mineral particles, organic matter, water, air and living organisms that supports plant growth
options.B: A type of rock formed by cooling magma
options.C: A mineral with a characteristic chemical composition

questions.explanation: Soil is a natural body of mineral particles, organic matter, water, air and living organisms that supports plant growth and develops through soil-forming processes.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What is soil formation?

options.A: The development of soil through weathering of parent material and the action of climate, organisms, relief/topography and time
options.B: The deposition of sediments by rivers
options.C: The cooling of magma beneath the surface
options.D: The precipitation of minerals from water

questions.explanation: Soil formation is the development of soil through weathering of parent material and the action of climate, organisms, relief/topography and time.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What are the major soil-forming factors?

options.A: Parent material, climate, organisms, relief or topography, and time

questions.explanation: The major soil-forming factors are parent material, climate, organisms, relief or topography, and time; human activity can also strongly modify soils.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What are soil horizons?

options.A: Distinct layers in a soil profile, commonly labelled O, A, E, B, C and R
options.B: Types of rocks found in soil

questions.explanation: Soil horizons are distinct layers in a soil profile, commonly labelled O, A, E, B, C and R where present; not every soil has all horizons.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What is humus?

options.A: The relatively stable, dark organic matter in soil formed by decomposition and transformation of plant and animal residues
options.B: A type of mineral found in rocks

questions.explanation: Humus is the relatively stable, dark organic matter in soil formed by decomposition and transformation of plant and animal residues.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What is the rock cycle?

options.A: The continuous set of processes by which igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks form and transform

questions.explanation: The rock cycle is the continuous set of processes by which igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks form and transform through melting, cooling, weathering, erosion, deposition, burial, heat and pressure.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: Can any rock type change into another rock type?

options.A: No, rocks cannot change type
options.B: Yes, through different geological processes, any rock group can be transformed into another

questions.explanation: Yes. Through different geological processes, any rock group can be transformed into another; the rock cycle has no single starting or ending point.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What is plate tectonics?

options.A: The theory that Earth's lithosphere is divided into moving plates that interact at boundaries
options.B: The study of rocks and minerals
options.C: The study of weather and climate
options.D: The study of water on Earth

questions.explanation: Plate tectonics is the theory that Earth's lithosphere is divided into moving plates that interact at boundaries and produce earthquakes, volcanism, mountain building and ocean-basin evolution.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What drives plate movement?

options.A: Only solar radiation
options.B: Mantle convection, gravitational sliding from elevated mid-ocean ridges and the pull of sinking slabs

questions.explanation: Plate motion is influenced by mantle convection, gravitational sliding from elevated mid-ocean ridges and the pull of sinking slabs; no single force explains every plate equally.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What is continental drift?

options.A: The idea that continents were once joined and have moved apart over geological time
options.C: The drift of clouds across the sky
options.D: The movement of tectonic plates only at divergent boundaries

questions.explanation: Continental drift is the idea proposed by Alfred Wegener that continents were once joined and have moved apart over geological time; modern plate tectonics explains the mechanism.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What was Pangaea?

options.A: A supercontinent in which most of Earth's landmasses were joined during the late Paleozoic and early Mesozoic eras
options.B: The first continent formed on Earth

questions.explanation: Pangaea was a supercontinent in which most of Earth's landmasses were joined during the late Paleozoic and early Mesozoic eras before breaking apart.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What evidence supports continental drift?

options.A: Only fossil evidence
options.B: The fit of continental margins, matching fossils and rock formations across oceans, ancient climate indicators and later evidence from seafloor spreading and paleomagnetism

questions.explanation: Evidence supporting continental drift includes the fit of continental margins, matching fossils and rock formations across oceans, ancient climate indicators and later evidence from seafloor spreading and paleomagnetism.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What are the three main types of plate boundaries?

options.A: Divergent, convergent and transform

questions.explanation: The three main types of plate boundaries are divergent, convergent and transform boundaries.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What happens at a divergent boundary?

options.A: Plates slide horizontally past each other
options.B: Plates move apart; magma may rise and create new oceanic crust at mid-ocean ridges or continental rift zones

questions.explanation: At a divergent boundary, plates move apart; magma may rise and create new oceanic crust at mid-ocean ridges or continental rift zones.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What happens at a convergent boundary?

options.A: Plates move apart and create new crust
options.B: Plates move towards one another; one plate may subduct beneath another, or continents may collide and build mountains
options.C: Plates slide horizontally past each other

questions.explanation: At a convergent boundary, plates move towards one another; one plate may subduct beneath another, or continents may collide and build mountains.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What happens at a transform boundary?

options.A: Plates move apart and create new crust
options.B: Plates move towards one another and subduct
options.C: Plates slide horizontally past each other, often producing earthquakes

questions.explanation: At a transform boundary, plates slide horizontally past each other, often producing earthquakes; crust is generally neither created nor destroyed.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What is subduction?

options.A: The process in which a denser lithospheric plate sinks beneath another plate into the mantle
options.B: The process of plates moving apart
options.C: The process of plates sliding past each other

questions.explanation: Subduction is the process in which a denser lithospheric plate sinks beneath another plate into the mantle, commonly producing trenches, earthquakes and volcanic arcs.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: How were the Himalayas formed?

options.A: By volcanic eruptions
options.B: The Indian Plate collided with the Eurasian Plate after the closure of the Tethys Ocean, compressing and uplifting sediments and crust

questions.explanation: The Himalayas formed when the Indian Plate collided with the Eurasian Plate after the closure of the Tethys Ocean, compressing and uplifting sediments and crust to form the Himalayas; convergence continues.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What is an earthquake?

options.A: Sudden ground shaking caused by the rapid release of accumulated elastic strain, usually along a fault

questions.explanation: An earthquake is sudden ground shaking caused by the rapid release of accumulated elastic strain, usually along a fault, generating seismic waves.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What is a fault?

options.A: A fracture or zone of fractures in Earth's crust along which rocks have moved relative to one another

questions.explanation: A fault is a fracture or zone of fractures in Earth's crust along which rocks have moved relative to one another.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What is the focus or hypocentre of an earthquake?

options.A: The point on Earth's surface directly above the earthquake
options.B: The point inside Earth where rupture begins
options.C: The instrument used to measure earthquakes
options.D: The scale used to measure earthquake magnitude

questions.explanation: The focus or hypocentre of an earthquake is the point inside Earth where rupture begins.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What is the epicentre of an earthquake?

options.A: The point inside Earth where rupture begins
options.B: The point on Earth's surface directly above the earthquake focus
options.C: The instrument used to measure earthquakes
options.D: The scale used to measure earthquake magnitude

questions.explanation: The epicentre is the point on Earth's surface directly above the earthquake focus.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What is the difference between magnitude and intensity?

options.A: Magnitude estimates the size of an earthquake at its source; intensity describes the observed shaking and damage at a particular location
options.B: Magnitude describes damage; intensity estimates size
options.D: Magnitude is measured in metres; intensity in kilograms

questions.explanation: Magnitude estimates the size of an earthquake at its source; intensity describes the observed shaking and damage at a particular location.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What is the Richter scale?

options.A: A historical local-magnitude scale developed for measuring certain earthquakes
options.B: A scale describing earthquake effects and shaking at locations

questions.explanation: The Richter scale is a historical local-magnitude scale developed for measuring certain earthquakes; modern seismology commonly uses moment magnitude for larger events.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What is moment magnitude?

options.A: A scale describing earthquake effects at locations
options.B: A logarithmic magnitude measure based on seismic moment, reflecting fault area, amount of slip and rock rigidity

questions.explanation: Moment magnitude is a logarithmic magnitude measure based on seismic moment, which reflects fault area, amount of slip and rock rigidity; it is widely used for earthquake size.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What is the Modified Mercalli Intensity scale?

options.A: A scale describing earthquake effects and shaking at locations, commonly expressed from I to XII

questions.explanation: The Modified Mercalli Intensity scale describes earthquake effects and shaking at locations, commonly expressed from I to XII.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What is an aftershock?

options.A: A smaller earthquake occurring after a larger mainshock in the same general region
options.B: An earthquake that precedes a larger event

questions.explanation: An aftershock is a smaller earthquake occurring after a larger mainshock in the same general region as the crust adjusts to the changed stress.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What is a foreshock?

options.A: A smaller earthquake occurring after a larger mainshock
options.B: An earthquake that precedes a larger event in the same area; it can only be identified as a foreshock after the larger earthquake occurs

questions.explanation: A foreshock is an earthquake that precedes a larger event in the same area; it can only be identified as a foreshock after the larger earthquake occurs.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: Can earthquakes be predicted exactly?

options.A: Yes, with modern technology
options.B: No reliable method can specify the exact time, place and magnitude of an earthquake

questions.explanation: No reliable method can specify the exact time, place and magnitude of an earthquake. Hazard assessment, monitoring, building codes and early-warning systems reduce risk.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What is a volcano?

options.A: An opening or landform through which magma, gases and volcanic material reach or approach Earth's surface

questions.explanation: A volcano is an opening or landform through which magma, gases and volcanic material reach or approach Earth's surface.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What is magma?

options.A: Molten or partially molten rock beneath Earth's surface
options.B: Magma that has reached Earth's surface

questions.explanation: Magma is molten or partially molten rock beneath Earth's surface.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What is lava?

options.A: Molten rock beneath Earth's surface
options.B: Magma that has reached Earth's surface

questions.explanation: Lava is magma that has reached Earth's surface.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What is the difference between active, dormant and extinct volcanoes?

options.A: Active volcanoes have erupted recently or show signs of activity; dormant volcanoes are quiet but may erupt again; extinct volcanoes are not expected to erupt again
options.B: Active volcanoes are large; dormant volcanoes are small; extinct volcanoes are medium-sized
options.C: Active volcanoes are underwater; dormant volcanoes are on land; extinct volcanoes are in space

questions.explanation: These are broad descriptive terms: active volcanoes have erupted in recent geological time or show signs of activity; dormant volcanoes are quiet but may erupt again; extinct volcanoes are not expected to erupt again. Definitions vary among scientific agencies.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What are shield volcanoes?

options.A: Steep-sided volcanoes built from alternating layers of lava and pyroclastic material
options.B: Broad volcanoes with gentle slopes, generally built by repeated flows of low-viscosity basaltic lava

questions.explanation: Shield volcanoes are broad volcanoes with gentle slopes, generally built by repeated flows of low-viscosity basaltic lava.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What are composite or stratovolcanoes?

options.A: Broad volcanoes with gentle slopes
options.B: Steep-sided volcanoes built from alternating layers of lava and pyroclastic material, often associated with subduction zones

questions.explanation: Composite or stratovolcanoes are steep-sided volcanoes built from alternating layers of lava and pyroclastic material, often associated with subduction zones.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What are volcanic hazards?

options.A: Lava flows, ash fall, pyroclastic density currents, lahars, volcanic gases, landslides and sometimes tsunamis

questions.explanation: Volcanic hazards include lava flows, ash fall, pyroclastic density currents, lahars, volcanic gases, landslides and sometimes tsunamis.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What is a tsunami?

options.A: A series of long-wavelength sea waves caused by sudden displacement of a large water volume
options.B: A type of tidal wave caused by the Moon

questions.explanation: A tsunami is a series of long-wavelength sea waves caused by sudden displacement of a large water volume, commonly by undersea earthquakes, but also by landslides or volcanic activity.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: Is a tsunami the same as a tidal wave?

options.A: Yes, they are identical
options.B: No, tsunamis are not caused by tides; the term tidal wave is misleading
options.C: Yes, both are caused by the Moon

questions.explanation: No. Tsunamis are not caused by tides; the term tidal wave is misleading.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: Why can a tsunami become dangerous near the coast?

options.A: Because the water becomes warmer
options.B: As water depth decreases, the wave slows and its height may increase

questions.explanation: As water depth decreases, the wave slows and its height may increase; coastal shape, bathymetry and local topography influence inundation.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What should people do after a tsunami warning?

options.A: Move immediately to higher ground or inland, follow official evacuation routes and alerts
options.B: Go to the beach to watch the waves
options.C: Stay in their homes near the coast

questions.explanation: After a tsunami warning, people should move immediately to higher ground or inland, follow official evacuation routes and alerts, and remain away from the coast until authorities declare it safe.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What is a landslide?

options.A: The downslope movement of rock, soil or debris under gravity

questions.explanation: A landslide is the downslope movement of rock, soil or debris under gravity, often triggered by intense rainfall, earthquakes, erosion, slope cutting or other disturbances.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What are common landslide types?

options.A: Falls, topples, slides, spreads and flows

questions.explanation: Common landslide types include falls, topples, slides, spreads and flows; debris flows and rockfalls are common examples.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: How can landslide risk be reduced?

options.A: Use hazard mapping, drainage management, slope stabilisation, vegetation where appropriate, regulated land use, monitoring and early warning
options.B: Build more houses on unstable slopes

questions.explanation: Landslide risk can be reduced by using hazard mapping, drainage management, slope stabilisation, vegetation where appropriate, regulated land use, monitoring and early warning; avoid unsafe construction on unstable slopes.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What is weathering?

options.A: The breakdown or alteration of rocks at or near Earth's surface by physical, chemical or biological processes
options.B: The transport of weathered material by water

questions.explanation: Weathering is the breakdown or alteration of rocks at or near Earth's surface by physical, chemical or biological processes, generally without transport of the material.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What is physical or mechanical weathering?

options.A: Rock breakdown without major chemical change, caused by processes such as freeze-thaw, thermal expansion, salt crystallisation and pressure release
options.B: The alteration of minerals through chemical reactions

questions.explanation: Physical or mechanical weathering is rock breakdown without major chemical change, caused by processes such as freeze-thaw, thermal expansion, salt crystallisation and pressure release.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What is chemical weathering?

options.A: Rock breakdown without major chemical change
options.B: The alteration or decomposition of minerals through chemical reactions such as hydrolysis, oxidation, carbonation and dissolution

questions.explanation: Chemical weathering is the alteration or decomposition of minerals through chemical reactions such as hydrolysis, oxidation, carbonation and dissolution.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What is biological weathering?

options.A: Rock breakdown without major chemical change
options.B: The alteration of minerals through chemical reactions
options.C: Rock breakdown or alteration caused by organisms, including root growth, burrowing and organic acids

questions.explanation: Biological weathering is rock breakdown or alteration caused by organisms, including root growth, burrowing and organic acids.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What is erosion?

options.A: The breakdown of rocks in place
options.B: The detachment and transport of weathered material by agents such as water, wind, ice and gravity

questions.explanation: Erosion is the detachment and transport of weathered material by agents such as water, wind, ice and gravity.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What is the difference between weathering and erosion?

options.A: Weathering breaks down or alters material in place; erosion removes and transports it
options.B: Weathering transports material; erosion breaks it down
options.D: Weathering only occurs in water; erosion only occurs on land

questions.explanation: Weathering breaks down or alters material in place; erosion removes and transports it.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What is deposition?

options.A: The breakdown of rocks in place
options.C: The settling or accumulation of transported sediment when the transporting agent loses energy or capacity

questions.explanation: Deposition is the settling or accumulation of transported sediment when the transporting agent loses energy or capacity.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What landforms are created by river deposition?

options.A: Floodplains, natural levees, alluvial fans, point bars and deltas

questions.explanation: Landforms created by river deposition include floodplains, natural levees, alluvial fans, point bars and deltas.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What is mountain building or orogeny?

options.A: The set of tectonic processes that form mountain belts, commonly involving plate convergence, folding, faulting, crustal thickening, metamorphism and magmatism
options.B: The erosion of mountains by rivers
options.C: The deposition of sediments in valleys

questions.explanation: Mountain building or orogeny is the set of tectonic processes that form mountain belts, commonly involving plate convergence, folding, faulting, crustal thickening, metamorphism and magmatism.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What is folding?

options.A: Bending of rock layers due to deformation, commonly under compressional stress
options.B: Fracturing and displacement of rock layers

questions.explanation: Folding is the bending of rock layers due to deformation, commonly under compressional stress.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What is faulting?

options.A: Bending of rock layers due to deformation
options.B: Fracturing and displacement of rock layers when stress exceeds rock strength

questions.explanation: Faulting is the fracturing and displacement of rock layers when stress exceeds rock strength.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What is the geological time scale?

options.A: A chronological framework that divides Earth's history into eons, eras, periods, epochs and ages

questions.explanation: The geological time scale is a chronological framework that divides Earth's history into eons, eras, periods, epochs and ages using geological, fossil and radiometric evidence.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What are the major divisions of geological time?

options.A: Eons, eras, periods, epochs and ages

questions.explanation: The largest divisions are eons; these are subdivided into eras, periods, epochs and ages.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: Name the four eons of Earth's history.

options.A: Hadean, Archean, Proterozoic and Phanerozoic

questions.explanation: The four eons of Earth's history are Hadean, Archean, Proterozoic and Phanerozoic.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What are the three eras of the Phanerozoic Eon?

options.A: Hadean, Archean and Proterozoic

questions.explanation: The three eras of the Phanerozoic Eon are Paleozoic, Mesozoic and Cenozoic.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What is the Mesozoic Era often called?

options.A: The Age of Mammals

questions.explanation: The Mesozoic Era is often called the Age of Reptiles, because dinosaurs and other reptiles were especially prominent.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What is the Cenozoic Era often called?

options.A: The Age of Reptiles

questions.explanation: The Cenozoic Era is often called the Age of Mammals, reflecting the diversification and prominence of mammals.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What is a natural geological hazard?

options.A: A potentially damaging geological process or event, such as an earthquake, volcanic eruption, tsunami, landslide, subsidence or avalanche

questions.explanation: A natural geological hazard is a potentially damaging geological process or event, such as an earthquake, volcanic eruption, tsunami, landslide, subsidence or avalanche.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What is the difference between a hazard and a disaster?

options.A: A hazard is a potentially harmful event or process; a disaster occurs when a hazard interacts with exposure and vulnerability and causes serious disruption and losses
options.B: A hazard causes damage; a disaster does not
options.D: A disaster is a natural event; a hazard is human-made

questions.explanation: A hazard is a potentially harmful event or process; a disaster occurs when a hazard interacts with exposure and vulnerability and causes serious disruption and losses.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What is seismic zoning in India?

options.A: India's seismic hazard is classified into zones II, III, IV and V in the commonly used BIS seismic zoning framework
options.B: India is divided into three seismic zones
options.D: India is divided into ten seismic zones

questions.explanation: India's seismic hazard is classified into zones II, III, IV and V in the commonly used BIS seismic zoning framework, with Zone V representing the highest seismic hazard category.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: Which parts of India have high earthquake hazard?

options.A: The Himalayan belt, Northeast India, Kutch region and parts of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands
options.D: The coastal plains of Tamil Nadu

questions.explanation: The Himalayan belt, Northeast India, Kutch region and parts of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands have significant seismic hazard; local risk depends on site conditions and vulnerability.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What is the Deccan volcanic province?

options.A: A large igneous province in western and central India formed by extensive basaltic lava eruptions near the end of the Cretaceous Period
options.B: A mountain range in southern India
options.C: A sedimentary basin in northern India
options.D: A desert region in western India

questions.explanation: The Deccan volcanic province is a large igneous province in western and central India formed by extensive basaltic lava eruptions near the end of the Cretaceous Period, producing the Deccan Traps.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What is the Barren Island volcano?

options.A: India's only confirmed active volcano, located in the Andaman Sea
options.B: A dormant volcano in the Himalayas
options.C: An extinct volcano in the Deccan Plateau
options.D: A volcano in the Arabian Sea

questions.explanation: Barren Island in the Andaman Sea is India's only confirmed active volcano; its activity is monitored by relevant scientific agencies.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Earth Science
questions.question: What is the role of the Geological Survey of India?

options.A: GSI conducts geological mapping, mineral-resource assessment, geoscientific research and studies related to landslides, earthquakes and other geological processes

questions.explanation: GSI conducts geological mapping, mineral-resource assessment, geoscientific research and studies related to landslides, earthquakes and other geological processes.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Meteorology
questions.question: What is meteorology?

options.A: The scientific study of the atmosphere and atmospheric processes, including weather and forecasting
options.B: The study of rocks and minerals
options.C: The study of water on Earth

questions.explanation: Meteorology is the scientific study of the atmosphere and atmospheric processes, including weather and forecasting.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Meteorology
questions.question: What is weather?

options.A: The long-term statistical pattern of atmospheric conditions
options.B: The short-term state of the atmosphere at a particular place and time

questions.explanation: Weather is the short-term state of the atmosphere at a particular place and time, including temperature, rainfall, humidity, wind, cloud and pressure.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Meteorology
questions.question: What is climate?

options.A: The short-term state of the atmosphere at a particular place and time
options.B: The long-term statistical pattern of weather in a region, usually assessed over standard periods such as 30 years

questions.explanation: Climate is the long-term statistical pattern of weather in a region, usually assessed over standard periods such as 30 years, along with variability and extremes.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Meteorology
questions.question: What is the atmosphere?

options.A: The envelope of gases surrounding Earth, held by gravity and essential for weather, climate and life
options.B: The solid outer layer of Earth
options.C: The water bodies on Earth's surface
options.D: The molten rock beneath Earth's surface

questions.explanation: The atmosphere is the envelope of gases surrounding Earth, held by gravity and essential for weather, climate and life.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Meteorology
questions.question: What are the main gases in dry air near Earth's surface?

options.A: Nitrogen about 78% and oxygen about 21%; argon about 0.93%; carbon dioxide and other trace gases make up the remainder
options.C: Carbon dioxide about 78% and oxygen about 21%

questions.explanation: Nitrogen is about 78% and oxygen about 21%; argon is about 0.93%, while carbon dioxide and other trace gases make up the remainder. Water vapour varies.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Meteorology
questions.question: What are the layers of the atmosphere?

options.A: Crust, mantle and core
options.B: Troposphere, stratosphere, mesosphere, thermosphere and exosphere

questions.explanation: The layers of the atmosphere are troposphere, stratosphere, mesosphere, thermosphere and exosphere, based mainly on temperature structure.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Meteorology
questions.question: What is the troposphere?

options.A: The lowest atmospheric layer, where most weather occurs and temperature generally decreases with height
options.B: The layer containing the ozone layer
options.C: The layer where meteors burn up

questions.explanation: The troposphere is the lowest atmospheric layer, where most weather occurs and temperature generally decreases with height.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Meteorology
questions.question: What is the stratosphere?

options.A: The lowest atmospheric layer where most weather occurs
options.B: The layer above the troposphere containing the ozone layer; temperature generally increases with height
options.C: The layer where meteors burn up

questions.explanation: The stratosphere is the layer above the troposphere containing the ozone layer; temperature generally increases with height because ozone absorbs ultraviolet radiation.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Meteorology
questions.question: What is the mesosphere?

options.A: The lowest atmospheric layer where most weather occurs
options.B: The layer containing the ozone layer
options.C: The atmospheric layer above the stratosphere where temperature generally decreases with height; many meteors burn up in this region

questions.explanation: The mesosphere is the atmospheric layer above the stratosphere where temperature generally decreases with height; many meteors burn up in this region.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Meteorology
questions.question: What is the thermosphere?

options.A: The lowest atmospheric layer where most weather occurs
options.B: The layer containing the ozone layer
options.C: The layer where meteors burn up
options.D: A high atmospheric layer in which temperature increases strongly with altitude due to absorption of high-energy solar radiation; auroras occur in this region

questions.explanation: The thermosphere is a high atmospheric layer in which temperature increases strongly with altitude due to absorption of high-energy solar radiation; auroras occur in this region.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Meteorology
questions.question: What is atmospheric pressure?

options.A: The force per unit area exerted by the weight and motion of air above a surface
options.B: The amount of water vapour in the air
options.C: The movement of air relative to Earth's surface

questions.explanation: Atmospheric pressure is the force per unit area exerted by the weight and motion of air above a surface.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Meteorology
questions.question: What is the standard atmospheric pressure at sea level?

options.A: Approximately 1013.25 hectopascals (hPa)

questions.explanation: Standard atmospheric pressure at sea level is approximately 1013.25 hectopascals (hPa), equivalent to 1 atmosphere or 760 mm of mercury.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Meteorology
questions.question: Which instrument measures atmospheric pressure?

options.A: Thermometer

questions.explanation: A barometer measures atmospheric pressure.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Meteorology
questions.question: What is humidity?

options.A: The amount of water vapour in the air
options.B: The force per unit area exerted by air
options.C: The movement of air relative to Earth's surface

questions.explanation: Humidity is the amount of water vapour in the air; it may be expressed as absolute humidity, specific humidity or relative humidity.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Meteorology
questions.question: What is relative humidity?

options.A: The ratio, expressed as a percentage, of the actual water-vapour pressure to the saturation vapour pressure at the same temperature
options.B: The total amount of water vapour in the air
options.C: The temperature at which air becomes saturated

questions.explanation: Relative humidity is the ratio, expressed as a percentage, of the actual water-vapour pressure to the saturation vapour pressure at the same temperature.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Meteorology
questions.question: Which instrument measures relative humidity?

options.A: Barometer

questions.explanation: A hygrometer measures relative humidity; a psychrometer uses wet- and dry-bulb thermometers to estimate humidity.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Meteorology
questions.question: What is temperature?

options.A: A measure of the thermal state of air, commonly measured in degrees Celsius in weather reports
options.B: The amount of water vapour in the air
options.C: The force per unit area exerted by air
options.D: The movement of air relative to Earth's surface

questions.explanation: Temperature is a measure of the thermal state of air, commonly measured in degrees Celsius in weather reports.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Meteorology
questions.question: Which instrument measures air temperature?

options.A: Barometer

questions.explanation: A thermometer measures air temperature, typically housed in a properly ventilated radiation screen for standard observations.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Meteorology
questions.question: What is wind?

options.A: The movement of air relative to Earth's surface, driven mainly by pressure differences
options.B: The amount of water vapour in the air
options.C: The force per unit area exerted by air

questions.explanation: Wind is the movement of air relative to Earth's surface, driven mainly by pressure differences and modified by Earth's rotation and surface friction.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Meteorology
questions.question: What is wind direction?

options.A: The direction in which the wind blows
options.B: The direction from which the wind blows, conventionally reported using compass points or degrees

questions.explanation: Wind direction is the direction from which the wind blows, conventionally reported using compass points or degrees.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Meteorology
questions.question: Which instrument measures wind speed?

options.A: Barometer

questions.explanation: An anemometer measures wind speed.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Meteorology
questions.question: Which instrument measures wind direction?

options.A: Anemometer

questions.explanation: A wind vane or wind direction sensor measures wind direction.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Meteorology
questions.question: What is the Coriolis effect?

options.A: The apparent deflection of moving air and water due to Earth's rotation: to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern Hemisphere
options.B: The warming of the atmosphere by the Sun
options.C: The cooling of air at high altitudes
options.D: The movement of air from high to low pressure

questions.explanation: The Coriolis effect is the apparent deflection of moving air and water due to Earth's rotation: to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern Hemisphere.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Meteorology
questions.question: What is a cloud?

options.A: A visible collection of tiny water droplets, ice crystals or both suspended in the atmosphere

questions.explanation: A cloud is a visible collection of tiny water droplets, ice crystals or both suspended in the atmosphere.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Meteorology
questions.question: What are the main cloud groups by form?

options.A: Cirrus, cumulus, stratus and nimbus-related forms

questions.explanation: The main cloud groups by form are cirrus, cumulus, stratus and nimbus-related forms; standard cloud genera include cirrus, cirrostratus, cirrocumulus, altostratus, altocumulus, stratus, stratocumulus, nimbostratus, cumulus and cumulonimbus.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Meteorology
questions.question: Which clouds are commonly associated with thunderstorms?

options.A: Cirrus clouds

questions.explanation: Cumulonimbus clouds are commonly associated with thunderstorms.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Meteorology
questions.question: What is precipitation?

options.A: Water released from clouds that falls to Earth's surface as rain, drizzle, snow, sleet or hail
options.B: The movement of air relative to Earth's surface
options.C: The amount of water vapour in the air
options.D: The force per unit area exerted by air

questions.explanation: Precipitation is water released from clouds that falls to Earth's surface as rain, drizzle, snow, sleet or hail.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Meteorology
questions.question: What is rainfall?

options.A: Liquid precipitation reaching the ground as raindrops

questions.explanation: Rainfall is liquid precipitation reaching the ground as raindrops.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Meteorology
questions.question: Which instrument measures rainfall?

options.A: Barometer

questions.explanation: A rain gauge measures rainfall.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Meteorology
questions.question: What is the monsoon?

options.A: A seasonal reversal or marked seasonal change in prevailing winds associated with land-sea thermal contrasts and large-scale atmospheric circulation

questions.explanation: The monsoon is a seasonal reversal or marked seasonal change in prevailing winds associated with land-sea thermal contrasts and large-scale atmospheric circulation; in South Asia it brings the major summer rainy season.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Meteorology
questions.question: What are the two main branches of the Indian southwest monsoon?

options.A: The Arabian Sea branch and the Bay of Bengal branch
options.B: The Pacific branch and the Atlantic branch
options.C: The Himalayan branch and the Deccan branch
options.D: The Western branch and the Eastern branch

questions.explanation: The two main branches of the Indian southwest monsoon are the Arabian Sea branch and the Bay of Bengal branch.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Meteorology
questions.question: When does the southwest monsoon normally reach Kerala?

options.A: Around 1 June

questions.explanation: The normal onset date of the southwest monsoon in Kerala is around 1 June, but actual onset varies from year to year and is officially declared by IMD using specified criteria.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Meteorology
questions.question: What is the northeast monsoon?

options.A: The post-monsoon seasonal circulation, generally during October-December, when northeasterly winds bring significant rainfall to Tamil Nadu and parts of southeast India

questions.explanation: The northeast monsoon is the post-monsoon seasonal circulation, generally during October-December, when northeasterly winds bring significant rainfall to Tamil Nadu and parts of southeast India.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Meteorology
questions.question: What is the Western Disturbance?

options.A: An eastward-moving extratropical weather system originating in the Mediterranean-West Asian region that brings winter rain and snowfall to northwestern India and the western Himalayas

questions.explanation: The Western Disturbance is an eastward-moving extratropical weather system originating in the Mediterranean-West Asian region that brings winter rain and snowfall to northwestern India and the western Himalayas.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Meteorology
questions.question: What is a tropical cyclone?

options.A: A rotating low-pressure weather system that forms over warm tropical or subtropical oceans and has organised thunderstorms and strong winds

questions.explanation: A tropical cyclone is a rotating low-pressure weather system that forms over warm tropical or subtropical oceans and has organised thunderstorms and strong winds.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Meteorology
questions.question: What conditions favour tropical cyclone formation?

options.A: Warm ocean water, sufficient atmospheric moisture and instability, low vertical wind shear, a pre-existing disturbance and enough Coriolis force away from the equator
options.B: Cold ocean water and high wind shear

questions.explanation: Conditions favouring tropical cyclone formation include warm ocean water, sufficient atmospheric moisture and instability, low vertical wind shear, a pre-existing disturbance and enough Coriolis force away from the equator.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Meteorology
questions.question: Why do tropical cyclones rarely form exactly at the equator?

options.A: Because the ocean is too cold
options.B: Because the Coriolis effect is too weak near the equator to provide the rotation needed for typical cyclone development
options.C: Because there is too much wind shear
options.D: Because the atmosphere is too dry

questions.explanation: Tropical cyclones rarely form exactly at the equator because the Coriolis effect is too weak near the equator to provide the rotation needed for typical cyclone development.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Meteorology
questions.question: What is the eye of a cyclone?

options.A: The relatively calm central region of a mature tropical cyclone, surrounded by the eyewall where the strongest winds and intense convection often occur
options.B: The outer edge of the cyclone

questions.explanation: The eye of a cyclone is the relatively calm central region of a mature tropical cyclone, surrounded by the eyewall where the strongest winds and intense convection often occur.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Meteorology
questions.question: What is an anticyclone?

options.A: A low-pressure system with surface convergence and rising air
options.B: A high-pressure system with air generally sinking and flowing outward near the surface

questions.explanation: An anticyclone is a high-pressure system with air generally sinking and flowing outward near the surface; circulation is clockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and anticlockwise in the Southern Hemisphere.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Meteorology
questions.question: What is the difference between a cyclone and an anticyclone?

options.A: A cyclone is a low-pressure system with surface convergence and rising air; an anticyclone is a high-pressure system with surface divergence and generally sinking air
options.B: A cyclone is a high-pressure system; an anticyclone is a low-pressure system
options.D: A cyclone occurs on land; an anticyclone occurs over the ocean

questions.explanation: A cyclone is a low-pressure system with surface convergence and rising air; an anticyclone is a high-pressure system with surface divergence and generally sinking air.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Meteorology
questions.question: What is weather forecasting?

options.A: The prediction of future atmospheric conditions using observations, numerical weather prediction models, statistical methods and expert interpretation

questions.explanation: Weather forecasting is the prediction of future atmospheric conditions using observations, numerical weather prediction models, statistical methods and expert interpretation.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Meteorology
questions.question: What is nowcasting?

options.A: Long-range forecasting for the next month
options.B: Short-range forecasting, generally for the next few hours, especially useful for thunderstorms, heavy rainfall, fog and severe weather

questions.explanation: Nowcasting is short-range forecasting, generally for the next few hours, especially useful for thunderstorms, heavy rainfall, fog and severe weather.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Meteorology
questions.question: What is numerical weather prediction?

options.A: The use of mathematical models of atmospheric physics and dynamics, initialised with observations, to forecast future weather
options.B: The use of statistical methods only
options.C: The use of expert interpretation only
options.D: The use of satellite observations only

questions.explanation: Numerical weather prediction is the use of mathematical models of atmospheric physics and dynamics, initialised with observations, to forecast future weather.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Meteorology
questions.question: What is a weather radar?

options.A: A remote-sensing instrument that uses radio waves to detect precipitation and estimate its location, movement and intensity
options.D: An instrument that measures wind speed

questions.explanation: A weather radar is a remote-sensing instrument that uses radio waves to detect precipitation and estimate its location, movement and intensity; Doppler radar can also estimate radial wind velocity.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Meteorology
questions.question: What is a radiosonde?

options.A: An instrument package carried by a weather balloon to measure upper-air variables such as temperature, pressure, humidity and wind
options.C: An instrument that measures wind speed
options.D: An instrument that measures atmospheric pressure

questions.explanation: A radiosonde is an instrument package carried by a weather balloon to measure upper-air variables such as temperature, pressure, humidity and wind.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Meteorology
questions.question: What is a weather satellite?

options.A: An artificial satellite that observes atmospheric and surface conditions using visible, infrared, microwave and other sensors
options.B: A natural satellite like the Moon

questions.explanation: A weather satellite is an artificial satellite that observes atmospheric and surface conditions using visible, infrared, microwave and other sensors.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Meteorology
questions.question: What is the difference between geostationary and polar-orbiting weather satellites?

options.A: Geostationary satellites remain above roughly the same equatorial longitude and provide frequent views of a region; polar-orbiting satellites pass over high latitudes and provide global coverage over time
options.B: Geostationary satellites orbit the poles; polar-orbiting satellites orbit the equator
options.C: They are the same type of satellite
options.D: Geostationary satellites are used for communication; polar-orbiting satellites are used for weather

questions.explanation: Geostationary satellites remain above roughly the same equatorial longitude and provide frequent views of a region; polar-orbiting satellites pass over high latitudes and provide global coverage over time.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Meteorology
questions.question: What is INSAT?

options.A: India's multipurpose satellite system that supports telecommunications, broadcasting and meteorological observation

questions.explanation: INSAT is India's multipurpose satellite system that supports telecommunications, broadcasting and meteorological observation; meteorological payloads provide cloud and weather information.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Meteorology
questions.question: What is the role of India's weather satellite system?

options.A: It supports monitoring of clouds, cyclones, water vapour and severe weather, improving forecasting, warning dissemination and disaster preparedness

questions.explanation: India's weather satellite system supports monitoring of clouds, cyclones, water vapour and severe weather, improving forecasting, warning dissemination and disaster preparedness.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Meteorology
questions.question: What is IMD?

options.A: The India Meteorological Department, established in 1875, is India's national meteorological service under the Ministry of Earth Sciences

questions.explanation: IMD is the India Meteorological Department, established in 1875, is India's national meteorological service under the Ministry of Earth Sciences.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Meteorology
questions.question: What are the major functions of IMD?

options.A: Weather observation and forecasting, cyclone and severe-weather warnings, climate services, meteorological data collection, monsoon monitoring and related services for aviation, agriculture and disaster management

questions.explanation: The major functions of IMD include weather observation and forecasting, cyclone and severe-weather warnings, climate services, meteorological data collection, monsoon monitoring and related services for aviation, agriculture and disaster management.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Meteorology
questions.question: What is the southwest monsoon onset declaration by IMD based on?

options.A: A single rainfall event
options.B: A set of objective criteria involving rainfall, wind and outgoing longwave radiation over specified areas

questions.explanation: The southwest monsoon onset declaration by IMD is based on a set of objective criteria involving rainfall, wind and outgoing longwave radiation over specified areas; it is not based on one rainfall event alone.
questions.source: Earth Science and Geological Science Study Guide

questions.subject: Meteorology
